name: Cherubism (SH3BP2)
aliases: familial fibrous dysplasia of the jaws

reference.source: Resnick's Diagnosis of Bone and Joint Disorders / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: Presents in early childhood with progressive, usually symmetrical, painless swelling of the jaws giving the characteristic full-cheeked cherubic facial appearance
Caused by autosomal dominant gain-of-function variants in SH3BP2, which enhance osteoclast activity and drive fibro-osseous replacement of the jaw bone
Radiographs show bilateral multilocular radiolucent, cyst-like expansile lesions of the mandible and maxilla
Histology reveals giant-cell-rich fibro-osseous lesions replacing normal jaw bone
The lesions are typically confined to the jaws and characteristically stabilise and often regress after puberty
Complications include dental disturbance with premature loss or displacement of teeth, and, in extensive maxillary disease, orbital involvement affecting the eyes
Management is often conservative with observation during the growth phase, reserving surgical contouring or curettage for functional or significant cosmetic problems, given the tendency to regress
reference.pathophysiology: Cherubism arises from autosomal dominant gain-of-function variants in SH3BP2, an adaptor protein that modulates signalling in cells of the myeloid and osteoclast lineage. The variants increase SH3BP2 stability and amplify downstream signalling, promoting excessive osteoclast formation and a local inflammatory, fibro-osseous process that replaces normal jaw bone with giant-cell-rich fibrous tissue. This produces the expansile, cyst-like lesions of the mandible and maxilla and the resulting facial swelling. The disease characteristically follows an age-dependent course, expanding through childhood, stabilising around puberty and frequently involuting thereafter as the abnormal osteoclastic drive subsides and the lesions ossify.
additionalDifferentials: Central giant-cell granuloma of the jaw
Fibrous dysplasia of the jaws (including polyostotic and McCune-Albright)
Aneurysmal bone cyst of the jaw
Noonan syndrome with multiple giant-cell lesions
Odontogenic keratocysts or other cystic jaw lesions
additionalInvestigations: Panoramic and cross-sectional jaw imaging demonstrating bilateral multilocular expansile lesions
Histological assessment where the diagnosis is uncertain, showing giant-cell fibro-osseous tissue
Serum calcium, phosphate and parathyroid hormone to exclude hyperparathyroidism and brown tumours
Dental and orthodontic assessment for tooth displacement and eruption problems
SH3BP2 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis and inform counselling
Ophthalmological and orbital assessment in extensive maxillary involvement
redFlags: Orbital or ophthalmic involvement threatening vision in extensive maxillary disease
Airway or feeding compromise from massive jaw expansion
Rapid or atypical growth raising concern for an alternative aggressive lesion
Persistent progression well beyond puberty, when regression is expected
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally favourable because the lesions tend to stabilise after puberty and often regress, leaving variable residual jaw deformity; extensive disease with orbital or airway involvement carries greater morbidity.
pitfalls: Undertaking aggressive surgery during the active childhood phase when many lesions regress spontaneously
Confusing cherubism with brown tumours of hyperparathyroidism without checking calcium and parathyroid hormone
Overlooking orbital involvement and vision risk in extensive maxillary disease
Failing to recognise the autosomal dominant inheritance and counsel the family
references: Resnick's Diagnosis of Bone and Joint Disorders
management: Watchful observation is appropriate for many, given the tendency of lesions to stabilise after puberty and often regress spontaneously
Surgical contouring or curettage for functionally or cosmetically significant deformity, ideally deferred until the active proliferative phase has subsided to reduce recurrence
Dental and orthodontic management of tooth displacement, failed eruption and premature tooth loss
Investigational antiresorptive therapy such as calcitonin or denosumab considered for aggressive, rapidly expanding disease
Urgent intervention for orbital involvement threatening vision or for airway compromise in extensive maxillary disease
Ophthalmology assessment where maxillary lesions encroach on the orbit
Multidisciplinary care across oral and maxillofacial surgery, metabolic bone medicine and clinical genetics
Genetic counselling for autosomal dominant SH3BP2 disease with family assessment
